new_statements.quote: El acento en tectiteco es predecible en lo que se refiere a los términos autóctonos, cayendo siempre en la última sílaba. Hay, no obstante, varios préstamos castellanos que llevan el acento en la penúltima sílaba; en la transcripción esto se indica mediante una tilde sobre la vocal acentuada (v.g. 8). [nota 5, p.16:] Hasta donde yo sé no hay sino dos excepciones a esta regla, a saber las dos variantes de los vocativos nóya y yéna, que se usan para dirigirse a niñas y a mujeres jóvenes. (Véase 1.2.2.11 más adelante).
new_statements.translation: Stress in Tectiteco is predictable as far as native words are concerned, always falling on the last syllable. There are, however, several Spanish loans that carry stress on the penultimate syllable; in the transcription this is indicated by an accent mark over the stressed vowel (e.g. 8). [note 5:] As far as I know there are only two exceptions to this rule, namely the two variants of the vocatives nóya and yéna, used to address girls and young women (see 1.2.2.11 below).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the final syllable of native words (Tectitán variety). Spanish loanwords may keep penultimate stress (written with an accent); the only native exceptions noted are the vocatives nóya / yéna with penultimate stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loans with penultimate stress (marked with a tilde in transcription); native vocatives nóya and yéna (notes 5 and 13) with penultimate stress. Note 4 quotes Beach 1980:55 that vowel duration varies with stress, glottal stop, laryngealisation and tone. NB: for the Mazapa (Chiapas) variety, Sobrino Gómez & Bennett (subm., pp.39-40, citing N. England p.c. 2019 and England & Baird 2017) report weight-sensitive stress instead: final by default, but the last long vowel attracts stress ([ˈɓiː.jaʔ] 'cañada'), and failing a long vowel a Vʔ syllable does ([ˈwáʔà.ɓeχ] 'tortilla'); Bennett 2016:495 reports plain final stress for Tectitán citing Pérez Vail 2007:37-8.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('términos autóctonos'); Stevenson gives no discussion of phrase-level effects and treats phonology only briefly (the work is a morphosyntactic sketch; vowel-length transcription called tentative). Data from Tectitán, Huehuetenango, fieldwork 1984-86.
new_statements.identity_note: Stevenson 1987 describes the Tectitán (Huehuetenango, Guatemala) variety, which he calls 'tectiteco' and distinguishes from Kaufman's Mexican 'teco'; same language, glottocode tekt1235 (no Glottolog dialect codes). The open second-hand report in Sobrino Gómez & Bennett (subm.) concerns the Mazapa de Madero (Chiapas, Mexico) variety and describes weight-sensitive (long vowel > Vʔ > final default) stress from N. England's data, so the two varieties/sources may genuinely differ or Stevenson's brief statement may under-describe weight effects (he notes vowel length is hard to hear and has minimal functional load in Tectitán).

sources.note: Sec. 1.1 'Los fonemas del tectiteco', p.4: stress is predictable in native words, always on the last syllable; several Spanish loans have penultimate stress, marked with a written accent. Note 5 (p.16): only two native exceptions known, the vocatives nóya and yéna; note 13 (p.17) repeats that these native words are exceptional in having penultimate stress. Note 4 quotes Beach 1980:55 that vowel length varies with stress, glottal stop, laryngealisation and tone 'como en otros dialectos mames'. Variety described: Tectitán, Huehuetenango, Guatemala.

sources.note: ms pp.39-40, ex. (22) 'Patrones acentuales en el teko de Mazapa': in Mazapa (Chiapas) Teko stress is weight-sensitive on a scale [Vː(C)] > [Vʔ] > {[VC],[V]}: final syllable by default ([pa.ˈt͡san]); if there is a long vowel, the syllable with the LAST long vowel ([ˈɓiː.jaʔ], [suː.ˈɓaːn]); with no long vowel, a [Vʔ] syllable ([ˈwáʔà.ɓeχ]), realised with a V́ʔV̀ contour; attributed to Nora England p.c. 2019 and England & Baird 2017. Second-hand report of England's field data.
WALS codes only feature 9A for Tectiteco (source Kaufman 1969:158), no stress features 14A-17A; StressTyp2 has no Tektiteko/Teco entry.
